## 2. On-call log entries

As required by section 9.1 of the handbook, every alert received during the shift has been recorded in the central on-call log. The table below reflects the exact entries recorded during the week.

| Timestamp (JST) | Service | Severity | First move | Summary and rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-03-19 14:22 | web | P3 | read logs | `web-4xx` fired after 4xx rate stayed slightly above 1 % for 10 minutes; logs showed recurring hits to an obsolete documentation route with zero customer tickets. |
| 2024-03-20 11:05 | notifier | P3 | no action | `notifier-queue-depth` briefly crossed threshold during an expected midday blast; delivered per minute remained healthy and cleared the backlog in 8 minutes. |
| 2024-03-21 16:40 | web | P3 | read logs | `web-4xx` fired a second time on the same obsolete documentation route; verified no origin errors or asset delivery failures before logging. |
| 2024-03-22 09:15 | api | P3 | no action | `api-partner-reject` blipped for partner sync testing under their contracted quota limit; traffic normalized without manual adjustment. |
| 2024-03-23 15:10 | payments | P3 | no action | `payments-webhook-retry` logged minor transient retries on settled card webhooks; all deliveries succeeded on first retry with zero customer checkout failures. |
| 2024-03-24 19:30 | web | P3 | no action | `web-traffic` alert triggered by legitimate Sunday evening consumer appointment search volume; error rates and page render latency remained flat. |

---

## 3. Notable alert investigations

### 3.1 `web-4xx` alert recurrence (renamed help route)

The only alert rule to trigger multiple times during the shift was `web-4xx`. Under section 14 of the handbook, `web-4xx` triggers when the 4xx HTTP response rate across the service exceeds 1 % for 10 consecutive minutes.

#### First occurrence (2024-03-19 14:22 JST)
- **Symptom:** The 4xx rate on the `Sorrel / web` dashboard nudged up to 1.18 % across nodes in ap-northeast-1.
- **Action taken:** The deploy history in the deploy tool for project "sorrel", service "web", showed the last deploy was `d-3841`, pushed 28 hours prior by Priya. Because the deploy was not recent, rolling back was not considered. I executed the first move `read logs` using the log search tool:
  ```text
  service=web status>=400 route=*
  ```
- **Findings:** The elevated status codes were almost entirely HTTP 404 responses targeting `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy`. A review of recent commits confirmed that our public support articles had been reorganized three days prior, moving this specific documentation article to `/help/appointments/reschedule`. External bookmarks, stale browser tabs, and cached external web links were requesting the previous path. 
- **Customer impact:** None. Booking flows, salon schedules, business calendar dashboards, and checkout sessions were unaffected. The core application routes had a 4xx error rate well below 0.2 %.
- **Severity assignment:** P3. Requests were served normally, and no operational function was broken.

#### Second occurrence (2024-03-21 16:40 JST)
- **Symptom:** The same alert rule fired again during the afternoon peak, reaching 1.09 % for 11 minutes.
- **Action taken:** I checked the `Sorrel / web` dashboard and repeated the log query to verify whether any new route had degraded. The errors remained identical: repeated requests to `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy`. Origin health was pristine, memory and CPU across the six nodes in each region were nominal, and edge metrics on the cloudflare dashboard confirmed no CDN asset failures.
- **Remediation & handoff:** Rather than leaving this route to flap the alert whenever public traffic spikes, I opened a backlog ticket (`WEB-1482`) assigned to Aiko's team. The ticket requests an explicit 301 permanent redirect from `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy` to `/help/appointments/reschedule`. Once deployed in a standard release, this will eliminate the redundant 404s and drop baseline 4xx metrics back below alerting thresholds.

### 3.2 Transient partner rejection on api (2024-03-22 09:15 JST)

On Friday morning, `api-partner-reject` triggered briefly for partner account `ptnr-772`. The alert condition evaluates when a single partner experiences rejections above 50 % over a 15-minute window.
- **Context:** Looking at the "Sorrel / api" board, the partner traffic panel revealed a burst of calendar synchronization calls exceeding their tier limit.
- **Action taken:** Under section 5.2 and section 17 of the handbook, on-call engineers never modify partner rate limits or contract tiers; limits are business agreements owned by Ravi and the partnerships team. I verified that the rejection responses were strictly HTTP 429 (rate limited) and that the rest of the partner endpoints, booking APIs, and customer endpoints were unaffected. 
- **Outcome:** The partner's script backed off within twelve minutes. The burn rate on our monthly booking SLO remained unaffected, replica lag was steady at 12 ms, and connection pools across the eight nodes in Tokyo were sitting at 28 % capacity. I logged the event as P3, first move `no action`, and informed Daniel (api engineer) during normal working hours.

### 3.3 Payments webhook retry rate (2024-03-23 15:10 JST)

On Saturday afternoon, an informational alert fired on `payments-webhook-retry` when the retry percentage reached 10.4 % over an hour.
- **Context:** The card provider (stripe) delivers signed webhook events to payments for charge confirmations, disputes, and refund lifecycle states. 
- **Investigation:** I opened the "Sorrel / payments" dashboard. The p95 checkout latency (ours) was steady at 180 ms, and the p95 provider response time was nominal at 410 ms. The refunds panel showed standard activity, and the webhook panel indicated that Stripe was sending minor bursts of re-deliveries.
- **Logs:** Searching `service=payments msg="webhook" outcome=retry` confirmed that our receivers were responding with 200 OK after idempotency checks, and the retried events were completely reconciled within two cycles. As noted in section 5.3 of the handbook, webhook retries without checkout drops are normal on busy days.
- **Outcome:** Recorded as P3, first move `no action`. Mei and Leo's weekly payout cron later ran without errors on Sunday night at 23:00 JST.

---

## 4. Seasonal traffic trends: March spring peak

Engineers taking the shift this week should be aware of seasonal patterns outlined in section 13.3 of the handbook.

### Spring school-term surge
March is traditionally an intense transition period in Japan. The conclusion of the academic year, graduations, and preparations for the school term starting in early April generate significant demand across specific merchant categories.
- **Tutor bookings:** Bookings for private tutors, test-prep academies, and academic instructors are currently up roughly 30 % compared to February volumes.
- **Other categories:** Hair salons and photography studios are similarly seeing elevated booking densities, whereas medical and physical therapy clinics are operating at standard seasonal baselines.

### Operational implications for `api` and database performance
1. **Monday morning write spikes (09:00–12:00 JST):**
   - Monday mornings represent the heaviest write volume of the week across Sorrel. Business owners open their web calendars, bulk-adjust available slots, confirm pending requests, and reschedule students.
   - With tutor volume elevated by 30 %, expect higher write throughput on api nodes and primary database instances in Tokyo (`ap-northeast`).
   - Keep an eye on the `Sorrel / api` dashboard:
     - **Database pool utilization:** Watch pool exhaustion metrics on the primary database instances. The connection pools across our eight nodes scale automatically between eight and twenty nodes if demand rises, but persistent slow queries can tie up connections.
     - **Replica lag:** Replica lag on read replicas normally sits under 30 ms. Ensure write bursts during slot creation do not drive replica lag up, which can cause read-after-write inconsistencies on booking pages.
     - **Search index freshness:** The slot search index ("find a slot near me") processes significantly higher invalidations when hundreds of recurring tutor lessons are scheduled simultaneously. Verify index freshness stays under 5 seconds.
2. **Evening checkout peaks (18:00–23:00 JST):**
   - Parents and students confirm bookings and pay deposits in the evening. Checkout submission rates will peak between 19:00 and 22:00 JST.
   - Watch the card provider response latency panel on `Sorrel / payments` alongside our internal checkout latency to quickly identify whether any slowdown originates inside our stack or upstream at stripe.

---

## 5. System status and health review

### 5.1 Service health matrix

| Service | Nodes (per region) | Deployment tool | Current status | Known quirks / Open items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **web** | 6–12 (autoscale) | deploy tool | Healthy | Ticket `WEB-1482` open for help page 301 redirect. Memory usage stable at ~42 % across all nodes. |
| **api** | 8–20 (autoscale) | deploy tool | Healthy | March tutor volume increasing write load. Connection pools healthy. Search latency p95 at 42 ms. |
| **payments** | 4 (fixed) | deploy tool | Healthy | Weekly payout completed cleanly on 2024-03-24 23:40 JST. Webhook idempotency layer fully nominal. |
| **notifier** | 3 workers + scheduler | deploy tool | Healthy | Nightly reminder batch (02:00–04:00 JST) peaks queue depth to ~650 messages, well below alerting thresholds. |

### 5.2 External provider status

All five external dependencies functioned reliably this week:
- **stripe (status.stripe.com):** Operational. No checkout timeouts, provider latency was stable under 450 ms throughout Friday and weekend checkout peaks.
- **twilio (status.twilio.com):** Operational. Carrier delivery across Japan mobile networks remained prompt. Sign-in SMS verification latency averaged 3.2 seconds.
- **sendgrid (status.sendgrid.com):** Operational. Email delivery rates hovered at 99.4 % with standard bounce rates. Daily vendor quota headroom remained above 45 %.
- **cloudflare (www.cloudflarestatus.com):** Operational. Edge cache hit ratio averaged 91.2 % on static assets. Origin fetch latency from Tokyo origin servers stayed below 15 ms.
- **aws (health.aws.amazon.com):** All systems green across `ap-northeast-1`, `us-east-1`, and `eu-west-1`. No networking degradation or storage alerts on our personal health dashboard.

---

## 6. Guidance for the incoming on-call (Leo)

As you begin your primary rotation, keep the following context in mind:

1. **Keep the five actions clear:**
   - Always remember the core decision framework from the handbook: *roll back*, *read logs*, *check provider*, *page owner*, or *no action*.
   - Never roll back a deploy that went out hours or days ago. If an alert fires on web or notifier, verify deploy age first. If the alert fires on payments and money has moved incorrectly, remember that rolling back is not the first move—paging Mei is.
2. **Monday morning slot rush:**
   - Watch the `Sorrel / api` dashboard between 09:00 and 12:00 JST today. If connection pools climb towards 80 %, check slow queries in the database panel. Use `service=api msg="pool exhausted"` in the log search tool to inspect bottlenecks before taking action.
   - Do not adjust partner limits if partners hit rate limits during synchronization; that remains an account governance decision for Ravi.
3. **Notifier batch behavior:**
   - If you see `notifier-queue-depth` climb between 02:00 and 04:00 JST, check `delivered per minute` before reacting. The scheduler loads the entire upcoming day's reminders for Japan during this window. If delivery throughput is healthy, let the queue drain naturally.
4. **Deploy hygiene:**
   - Deploys are prohibited between 22:00 and 07:00 JST, on Friday afternoons after 16:00 JST, or during provider maintenance windows. Regular deploys across teams are typically scheduled on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.
5. **Open tickets to track:**
   - `WEB-1482`: Adding 301 redirect for the legacy help page to prevent further `web-4xx` alert triggers. Aiko's team has this in their sprint.

---

## 7. Sign-off and handover confirmation

Handover conducted via `#on-call` and the incident management schedule on Monday, 2024-03-25 at 10:00 JST.

- **Incoming primary:** Leo (payments) — *Confirmed and taken*

## 3. Notable alert investigations

### 3.1 `web-4xx` alert recurrence (renamed help route)

The only alert rule to trigger multiple times during the shift was `web-4xx`. Under section 14 of the handbook, `web-4xx` triggers when the 4xx HTTP response rate across the service exceeds 1 % for 10 consecutive minutes.

#### First occurrence (2024-03-19 14:22 JST)
- **Symptom:** The 4xx rate on the `Sorrel / web` dashboard nudged up to 1.18 % across nodes in ap-northeast-1.
- **Action taken:** The deploy history in the deploy tool for project "sorrel", service "web", showed the last deploy was `d-3841`, pushed 28 hours prior by Priya. Because the deploy was not recent, rolling back was not considered. I executed the first move `read logs` using the log search tool:
  ```text
  service=web status>=400 route=*
  ```
- **Findings:** The elevated status codes were almost entirely HTTP 404 responses targeting `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy`. A review of recent commits confirmed that our public support articles had been reorganized three days prior, moving this specific documentation article to `/help/appointments/reschedule`. External bookmarks, stale browser tabs, and cached external web links were requesting the previous path. 
- **Customer impact:** None. Booking flows, salon schedules, business calendar dashboards, and checkout sessions were unaffected. The core application routes had a 4xx error rate well below 0.2 %.
- **Severity assignment:** P3. Requests were served normally, and no operational function was broken.

#### Second occurrence (2024-03-21 16:40 JST)
- **Symptom:** The same alert rule fired again during the afternoon peak, reaching 1.09 % for 11 minutes.
- **Action taken:** I checked the `Sorrel / web` dashboard and repeated the log query to verify whether any new route had degraded. The errors remained identical: repeated requests to `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy`. Origin health was pristine, memory and CPU across the six nodes in each region were nominal, and edge metrics on the cloudflare dashboard confirmed no CDN asset failures.
- **Remediation & handoff:** Rather than leaving this route to flap the alert whenever public traffic spikes, I opened a backlog ticket (`WEB-1482`) assigned to Aiko's team. The ticket requests an explicit 301 permanent redirect from `/help/booking/rescheduling-policy` to `/help/appointments/reschedule`. Once deployed in a standard release, this will eliminate the redundant 404s and drop baseline 4xx metrics back below alerting thresholds.

### 3.2 Transient partner rejection on api (2024-03-22 09:15 JST)

On Friday morning, `api-partner-reject` triggered briefly for partner account `ptnr-772`. The alert condition evaluates when a single partner experiences rejections above 50 % over a 15-minute window.
- **Context:** Looking at the "Sorrel / api" board, the partner traffic panel revealed a burst of calendar synchronization calls exceeding their tier limit.
- **Action taken:** Under section 5.2 and section 17 of the handbook, on-call engineers never modify partner rate limits or contract tiers; limits are business agreements owned by Ravi and the partnerships team. I verified that the rejection responses were strictly HTTP 429 (rate limited) and that the rest of the partner endpoints, booking APIs, and customer endpoints were unaffected. 
- **Outcome:** The partner's script backed off within twelve minutes. The burn rate on our monthly booking SLO remained unaffected, replica lag was steady at 12 ms, and connection pools across the eight nodes in Tokyo were sitting at 28 % capacity. I logged the event as P3, first move `no action`, and informed Daniel (api engineer) during normal working hours.

### 3.3 Payments webhook retry rate (2024-03-23 15:10 JST)

On Saturday afternoon, an informational alert fired on `payments-webhook-retry` when the retry percentage reached 10.4 % over an hour.
- **Context:** The card provider (stripe) delivers signed webhook events to payments for charge confirmations, disputes, and refund lifecycle states. 
- **Investigation:** I opened the "Sorrel / payments" dashboard. The p95 checkout latency (ours) was steady at 180 ms, and the p95 provider response time was nominal at 410 ms. The refunds panel showed standard activity, and the webhook panel indicated that Stripe was sending minor bursts of re-deliveries.
- **Logs:** Searching `service=payments msg="webhook" outcome=retry` confirmed that our receivers were responding with 200 OK after idempotency checks, and the retried events were completely reconciled within two cycles. As noted in section 5.3 of the handbook, webhook retries without checkout drops are normal on busy days.
- **Outcome:** Recorded as P3, first move `no action`. Mei and Leo's weekly payout cron later ran without errors on Sunday night at 23:00 JST.

## 4. Seasonal traffic trends: March spring peak

Engineers taking the shift this week should be aware of seasonal patterns outlined in section 13.3 of the handbook.

### Spring school-term surge
March is traditionally an intense transition period in Japan. The conclusion of the academic year, graduations, and preparations for the school term starting in early April generate significant demand across specific merchant categories.
- **Tutor bookings:** Bookings for private tutors, test-prep academies, and academic instructors are currently up roughly 30 % compared to February volumes.
- **Other categories:** Hair salons and photography studios are similarly seeing elevated booking densities, whereas medical and physical therapy clinics are operating at standard seasonal baselines.

### Operational implications for `api` and database performance
1. **Monday morning write spikes (09:00–12:00 JST):**
   - Monday mornings represent the heaviest write volume of the week across Sorrel. Business owners open their web calendars, bulk-adjust available slots, confirm pending requests, and reschedule students.
   - With tutor volume elevated by 30 %, expect higher write throughput on api nodes and primary database instances in Tokyo (`ap-northeast`).
   - Keep an eye on the `Sorrel / api` dashboard:
     - **Database pool utilization:** Watch pool exhaustion metrics on the primary database instances. The connection pools across our eight nodes scale automatically between eight and twenty nodes if demand rises, but persistent slow queries can tie up connections.
     - **Replica lag:** Replica lag on read replicas normally sits under 30 ms. Ensure write bursts during slot creation do not drive replica lag up, which can cause read-after-write inconsistencies on booking pages.
     - **Search index freshness:** The slot search index ("find a slot near me") processes significantly higher invalidations when hundreds of recurring tutor lessons are scheduled simultaneously. Verify index freshness stays under 5 seconds.
2. **Evening checkout peaks (18:00–23:00 JST):**
   - Parents and students confirm bookings and pay deposits in the evening. Checkout submission rates will peak between 19:00 and 22:00 JST.
   - Watch the card provider response latency panel on `Sorrel / payments` alongside our internal checkout latency to quickly identify whether any slowdown originates inside our stack or upstream at stripe.

# On-call handover, week of 2025-01-06

Last updated: 2025-01-06 10:00 JST  
Owner: Yuki (notifier), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Daniel (api)  

---

## 1. Shift summary

The shift ran from Monday 2024-12-30 10:00 JST through Monday 2025-01-06 10:00 JST. Overall, this was a relatively quiet week on the paging front because production was under the scheduled year-end deploy freeze (26 December to 4 January), which lifted at the end of the day on Saturday, 4 January. 

No P1 or P2 incidents occurred during the rotation. Across all regions (`ap-northeast`, `us-east`, `eu-west`), services operated within target SLOs. Background batch workloads behaved normally over the holiday: the weekly payout run executed as scheduled on Sunday 23:00 JST without paging, and the daily reminder schedules completed inside their standard windows.

The primary operational event of note was the scheduled New Year bulk greeting dispatch on 2025-01-01, along with a creeping disk alert on one of the `web` nodes that requires attention early this week.

---

## 2. Service-by-service operational status

### 2.1 web
- **Status:** Healthy across all regions (`ap-northeast-1`, `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`).
- **Traffic and latency:** Server-side p95 render times averaged 420 ms; edge performance via Cloudflare remained steady with cache hit ratios hovering around 86 % for static assets.
- **Node health:** All 6 nodes in `ap-northeast` remained in service without unexpected restarts. However, node 4 in `ap-northeast` approached the disk warning threshold on Sunday afternoon. Details and ticket tracking are noted in section 5.
- **Admin tool:** Normal operational traffic. Hana's support team logged standard account inquiry lookups and single-confirmation resends; no bulk actions or deletion anomalies were triggered.

### 2.2 api
- **Status:** Healthy across all three regions.
- **SLO & latency:** Error budget consumption was negligible (<0.1 % of monthly budget used). Request latency across endpoint groups remained stable:
  - Booking: p95 at 210 ms.
  - Search: p95 at 340 ms.
  - Account: p95 at 110 ms.
  - Partner: p95 at 180 ms.
- **Database & cache:** Primary connection pool utilization peaked at 48 % during the lunch booking window on Friday. Replica lag remained under 12 ms across all read replicas. Search index freshness remained within bounds, and audit writer logs confirmed uninterrupted writes.
- **Partners:** All major partner integrations operated within their contractual limits. No rate limiting or 429 bursts occurred.

### 2.3 payments
- **Status:** Healthy.
- **Checkout & provider metrics:** Checkout failure rate remained well below 0.1 %. The p95 checkout latency hovered at 1.4 s, with provider processing latency at Stripe averaging 980 ms. 
- **Webhooks & reconciliation:** Webhook retries stayed within baseline parameters (under 1.5 % over the week), driven by normal transient network retransmissions that completed successfully on retry.
- **Payout job:** The Sunday 23:00 JST payout run completed in 37 minutes with zero unhandled exceptions. Mei and Leo monitored the batch.

### 2.4 notifier
- **Status:** Healthy.
- **Queue and workers:** Queue depths followed the expected seasonal pattern: overnight rises between 02:00 and 04:00 JST for the scheduled reminder batch, followed by steady draining prior to 06:00 JST.
- **New Year dispatches:** Detailed in section 3 below. SMS traffic via Twilio and transactional email via SendGrid stayed within daily quota allowances. No duplicate dispatch IDs were flagged on the duplicate detection panel.

---

## 3. Notable events during the shift

### 3.1 New Year greeting batch (2025-01-01)
Businesses on Sorrel frequently schedule annual greeting messages and updated holiday operating schedules for their client lists on New Year's Day.

- **Execution:** Between 00:30 JST and 04:00 JST on 2025-01-01, `notifier` queued and successfully delivered 41,000 New Year greeting emails for businesses on the platform.
- **Queue behavior:** Messages were staged on the background queue and processed by the worker fleet (3 worker nodes per active region). Queue depth temporarily peaked at 3,420 items around 01:15 JST, but worker delivery rate sustained ~310 emails per minute across providers.
- **Vendor handling:** SendGrid accepted all dispatches without quota rejections or 429 throttling. No vendor errors or bounce spikes occurred, and delivery confirmation callbacks returned clean. No pager alerts fired, and customer notifications proceeded without trouble.

### 3.2 Post-freeze queue accumulation
Because deploys were frozen from 26 December through 4 January, engineers across teams have accumulated tested branches awaiting production release. The deploy freeze ended over the weekend. 

- As expected for the first week back, the deploy tool queue is heavily loaded with changes across `web`, `api`, `payments`, and `notifier`.
- Teams have scheduled rollouts for normal release windows, so expect heavy deploy traffic on Tuesday and Thursday afternoon.

---

## 4. On-call log entries for the week

Below is the single alert that required evaluation during the week, recorded in the on-call log per handbook standard:

| Date | Time (JST) | Service | Severity | First Move | Reason & Action Taken |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-05 | 16:42 | `web` | P3 | no action | Disk utilization on `ap-northeast` node 4 reached 78 % (threshold for alert is 80 %). Examined rate of rise; render cache growth is linear and will not cross threshold before Monday working hours. Logged ticket for owning team. |

---

## 5. Ongoing issues and watch items

### 5.1 `web` node 4 disk usage (`web-disk` alert watch)
- **Symptom:** On Sunday afternoon, disk usage on `node-web-04` in `ap-northeast-1` was observed climbing to 78 %, just below the 80 % paging threshold defined by the `web-disk` alert rule.
- **Root cause check:** Inspected the filesystem breakdown on the node. The root volume disk usage is driven by accumulated local server-side render cache artifacts (`/var/cache/sorrel/render`) and retained log chunks that have not rotated through standard garbage collection.
- **Current status:** Disk consumption has stabilized around 78.4 % as of Monday 09:30 JST. The other five web nodes in the region are currently sitting between 54 % and 62 % disk utilization. Node 4 is serving customer traffic normally and is not experiencing OOM events or memory heap pressure.
- **Action taken:** Opened ticket `WEB-1842` for Aiko's team to execute the standard render cache cleanup routine and verify log rotation configurations on that node during working hours.
- **Instructions for incoming on-call (Daniel):**
  - If node 4 touches 80 % before Aiko or Priya take the ticket, `web-disk` will page.
  - Review dashboard "Sorrel / web" -> panel "Disk usage per node".
  - If the alert fires and the trend remains slow, note the metric in the on-call log and follow up in `#team-web`. If disk growth accelerates rapidly or causes node instability, remember that node replacement or manual filesystem intervention must follow the standard runbook, with Aiko paged only if decisions outside on-call authority are required.

### 5.2 Heavy deploy calendar (Tuesday and Thursday)
- **Context:** As this is the first full working week following the year-end freeze, engineers are eager to ship updates that were held back over the holidays.
- **Expected activity:**
  - Tuesday (2025-01-07) afternoon: Deploys planned for `api` (Daniel / Ravi) and `web` (Aiko / Priya).
  - Thursday (2025-01-09) afternoon: Secondary changes planned for `payments` (Mei / Leo) and `notifier` (Tom / Yuki).
- **Reminders for Daniel:**
  - Standard deploy rules apply (Handbook section 11): deploys are one service at a time, peer-reviewed, and restricted to the hours between 07:00 and 22:00 JST. No deploys should occur after 16:00 on Friday.
  - Watch for immediate regressions within the first 30 minutes following any rollout. If a symptom starts immediately following a deploy, check deploy age on the alert line and verify boards before taking action.
  - The deploy tool maintains the previous twenty deploys for every service. A rollback for `web` or `notifier` takes about three to four minutes and re-points nodes two at a time; `web` also re-points CDN static asset sets on Cloudflare. For `api` and `payments`, refer directly to their respective service runbooks and guidelines.
  - If an issue is deploy-related and meets the criteria, execute the rollback to the previous release, write both deploy IDs in the incident thread, and update the log.

---

| **Cloudflare** | Edge CDN, WAF, public SSL | `www.cloudflarestatus.com` | Operational globally. Tokyo edge nodes reporting normal response times and low origin fetch latencies. |
| **Stripe** | Checkout charges, refunds, payouts | `status.stripe.com` | Operational. Webhook delivery latencies within normal range (<2 s). |
| **Twilio** | SMS sign-in codes, appointment reminders | `status.twilio.com` | Operational. Japanese carrier delivery routes reporting 100 % message delivery acceptance. |
| **SendGrid** | Transactional booking emails, notifications | `status.sendgrid.com` | Operational. Zero queueing backlog or vendor error codes logged over the past 24 hours. |

## 7. Operational reminders and reference links

For quick reference during your shift, keep the standard tools and handbook locations pinned:

- **Incident coordination:** `#inc-live` in chat. Remember: open a thread for any P1 or P2, paste the alert line directly at the top, and log the first move before undertaking multi-minute diagnostics.
- **Dashboards:** Folder "Sorrel / Services" on the metrics tool:
  - Web: "Sorrel / web" (watch 5xx, p95 load times, edge CDN errors, node disk usage).
  - API: "Sorrel / api" (watch endpoint latencies, DB pool saturation, audit log writes, partner rejection rates).
  - Payments: "Sorrel / payments" (watch checkout submission failures, provider timeout vs. local latency, duplicate refund counts).
  - Notifier: "Sorrel / notifier" (watch queue depth vs. delivered per minute, vendor response codes, duplicate message detection).
- **Logs:** Index `sorrel-prod-*`. Always narrow search windows to the exact alert onset to conserve search cluster capacity. Common error filters:
  - `service=web level=ERROR`
  - `service=api msg="pool exhausted"`
  - `service=payments outcome=failed`
  - `service=notifier msg="vendor error"`
- **Handbook first moves:** As a reminder, apply only one of the five approved first moves:
  1. *roll back:* When a recent deploy of that service is the direct cause.
  2. *read logs:* When nobody knows yet what happened.
  3. *check provider:* When the alert itself indicates an outside service dependency issue.
  4. *page owner:* When an irreversible state has occurred (money moved incorrectly, data exposed, credentials leaked, accounts deleted) or when an unpermitted decision must be made.
  5. *no action:* When no customer impact is present and no system has failed.

---

- **Shift transfer time:** 2025-01-06 10:00 JST  
- **Outgoing primary:** Yuki (notifier)  
- **Incoming primary:** Daniel (api)  
- **Secondary on-call for this week:** Sara (platform engineer)

## 4. Detailed Event Reviews

### Event 1: Morning Peak `api-pool` Alerts (2025-06-26)

- **Timing**: 
  - First alert: 2025-06-26 09:18 JST (cleared 09:30 JST)
  - Second alert: 2025-06-26 10:04 JST (cleared 10:15 JST)
- **Service**: `api`
- **Region**: `ap-northeast` (Tokyo)
- **Initial Severity**: P2
- **First Move**: `read logs`

#### Context & Timeline
Thursday morning marks one of the heaviest weekly booking and calendar modification periods in `ap-northeast`. Businesses open their operational dashboards between 09:00 and 10:00 JST, reviewing reservations, updating staff rosters, and confirming schedules while commuters book appointments simultaneously.

At 09:18 JST, the `api-pool` alert rule fired for node `api-apne1-node-03`, indicating connection pool utilization had crossed the 90% threshold for 10 minutes (peaking at 92.4%). 

Because the symptoms showed connection pool saturation rather than an immediate bad deploy (the last `api` deploy was `d-3841`, pushed two days prior on Tuesday afternoon), the first move was **read logs** per Section 3.2. 

Querying `sorrel-prod-*` for `service=api msg="pool exhausted"` showed no hard pool exhaustion errors or dropped incoming requests, but indicated that database connections were being held longer than usual. Cross-referencing the "Sorrel / api" dashboard showed:
- Database query times on primary read replicas ticked up slightly (p95 moving from 45ms to 180ms).
- Primary connection pool utilization was clustered tightly around nodes handling business calendar writes.
- 5xx error rate remained flat (<0.02%), and the monthly SLO error budget panel showed zero material burn.

By 09:30 JST (12 minutes after the alert fired), connection utilization dropped back down to 74% as the 09:00 burst subsided, and the alert cleared automatically.

At 10:04 JST, a second alert fired on node `api-apne1-node-06`, peaking at 91.1% pool capacity. Following the same protocol, I checked `service=api` logs and the database panel. We observed a secondary concurrency burst on slot availability lookups. No pool acquisition timeouts (`msg="pool exhausted"`) occurred. The pool leveled off and cleared at 10:15 JST (11 minutes duration).

#### Outcome & Next Steps
Neither incident degraded booking requests for customers or businesses, and no requests timed out. However, the connection pool headroom during peak Tokyo morning business hours is narrower than comfortable as platform booking volume has grown over the past quarter. 

I discussed the metrics with Ravi (api owner) during working hours on Thursday afternoon. Increasing the connection pool per node requires evaluating database primary memory and client limits across our autoscaling ceiling (up to 20 nodes in `ap-northeast`). Ravi opened an engineering ticket to benchmark and raise the pool allocation per node ahead of the July traffic baseline.

---

- **Service**: `api`
- **Region**: Global / `ap-northeast`
- **Initial Severity**: P3
- **First Move**: `no action`

#### Context & Timeline

Following Section 7.9 (Noisy but harmless traffic):

The re-sync concluded at approximately 12:15 JST, and request volume returned to normal weekend baseline levels by 12:20 JST. I documented the volume spike in the on-call log and confirmed that no alert tuning was necessary, as the partner behaved well within system constraints.

On Wednesday 2026-04-01 and Thursday 2026-04-02, Sorrel experienced sustained traffic peaks driven heavily by tutoring academies, music teachers, and hair salons.

- **api performance:** The morning write peak on `api` between 07:00 and 09:00 JST on both days saw booking creation rates rise to approximately 2.6x normal weekday baselines. The search index for "find a slot near me" handled elevated query loads without replica lag or query timeouts. Connection pools on all eight nodes in `ap-northeast` remained below 68% utilization (alert threshold: 90% for 10 minutes). The monthly error budget for booking endpoints was essentially untouched.
- **payments checkout:** The checkout flow saw heavy volume during the secondary evening peak (18:00–23:00 JST). Checkout failure rates stayed flat between 0.1% and 0.3%, well below the 2% threshold. Provider response times from stripe remained healthy throughout the burst, and webhook deliveries processed cleanly.
- **notifier queues:** The scheduler queued substantial reminder batches between 02:00 and 04:00 JST. Queue depth reached roughly 780 messages at its highest overnight point on 2026-04-02, safely below the 1,000-message `notifier-queue-depth` threshold. Workers drained the backlog steadily before 05:30 JST, and delivery rates on twilio (SMS reminders) and sendgrid (booking confirmations) remained within normal operational latency.
- **Outcome:** Zero alerts fired during the two-day traffic peak.

### 3.2 Alert detail: web-traffic (2026-04-03)

- **Timestamp:** 2026-04-03 14:22 JST
- **Rule:** `web-traffic` (Request volume above 3x the same hour last week for 15 minutes)
- **Severity:** P3
- **First move:** `no action`

#### What happened
At 14:22 JST on Friday afternoon, the `web-traffic` alert fired for `ap-northeast`. Total inbound request volume to `web` spiked to approximately 3.4x the baseline measured at 14:00 JST the previous Friday.

#### Checks conducted
1. **Board review:** Checked the "Sorrel / web" dashboard. The status class breakdown showed a spike concentrated purely in `2xx` and `304` responses. The edge cache hit ratio on cloudflare absorbed roughly 62% of the initial hit, but origin requests rose sufficiently to cross the three-fold threshold.
2. **Customer experience:** Server-side p95 page load remained steady at 240 ms (well below the 2 s threshold). Browser-reported script errors and blank render metrics were completely clean. 5xx rate was 0.01%.
3. **Log inspection:** Ran a targeted search on `sorrel-prod-*` (`service=web status=200 route="/b/*"`). The request stream originated from an automated indexing crawler traversing public merchant landing pages and salon service menus.
4. **api health:** Checked "Sorrel / api" to ensure crawler traffic was not cascading into un-cached database queries. The search index and read replicas showed no elevation in query latency.

#### Disposition
Because requests were being served cleanly, no errors were generated, no internal safety nets were degraded, and zero customers were impacted, this was classified as a P3 (handbook section 2). In line with handbook section 3.5 and section 7.9 (Noisy but harmless traffic), the appropriate first move was `no action`. A line was logged, and a low-priority Jira ticket (`PLAT-4192`) was filed for Aiko to consider refining crawler rate limits on cloudflare during regular working hours.

Provider response times from stripe remained healthy throughout the burst, and webhook deliveries processed cleanly.

- **Severity:** P3
- **First move:** `no action`

#### What happened
At 14:22 JST on Friday afternoon, the `web-traffic` alert fired for `ap-northeast`. Total inbound request volume to `web` spiked to approximately 3.4x the baseline measured at 14:00 JST the previous Friday.

#### Checks conducted
1. **Board review:** Checked the "Sorrel / web" dashboard. The status class breakdown showed a spike concentrated purely in `2xx` and `304` responses. The edge cache hit ratio on cloudflare absorbed roughly 62% of the initial hit, but origin requests rose sufficiently to cross the three-fold threshold.
2. **Customer experience:** Server-side p95 page load remained steady at 240 ms (well below the 2 s threshold). Browser-reported script errors and blank render metrics were completely clean. 5xx rate was 0.01%.

4. **api health:** Checked "Sorrel / api" to ensure crawler traffic was not cascading into un-cached database queries. The search index and read replicas showed no elevation in query latency.

Because requests were being served cleanly, no errors were generated, no internal safety nets were degraded, and zero customers were impacted, this was classified as a P3 (handbook section 2). In line with handbook section 3.5 and section 7.9 (Noisy but harmless traffic), the appropriate first move was `no action`. # stripe: notes for on-call

Date: 2024-07-08  
Author: Mei (payments owner)  
Target audience: Platform team, SRE, and primary/secondary on-call rotation  

---

## 1. Context and Purpose

Sorrel operates four core services: `web`, `api`, `payments`, and `notifier`. Of these four, `payments` is the single service that communicates with Stripe. 

We process customer card transactions whenever appointments require upfront deposits or full prepayment. In addition to customer checkouts, `payments` issues refunds when appointments are cancelled inside a merchant's designated cancellation window, and handles the Sunday weekly payout run that disburses funds to businesses across our three active cloud regions: `ap-northeast` (Tokyo), `us-east`, and `eu-west`.

Because `payments` handles real money, operational mistakes can lead to irreversible state changes, incorrect ledger entries, or customer financial harm. This note covers the architectural boundary between Sorrel and Stripe, what failure modes look like from our dashboards, how webhooks behave over time, and what actions on-call engineers are strictly permitted—and forbidden—to take when Stripe is degraded or failing.

---

## 2. Core Operational Rules for On-Call

When on-call engineers respond to alerts involving checkout failures, refund anomalies, or webhook backlogs, keep the following hard constraints in mind:

1. **Check status.stripe.com first.**  
   `status.stripe.com` is the status page; subscribe the incident thread to it during a payments incident. When external calls fail or time out while our own application nodes are healthy, verify Stripe's upstream platform health before touching anything internally.
2. **Never change anything in the stripe dashboard during an incident.**  
   Payment settings are Mei's decision. On-call engineers have read-only visibility into operational metrics and logs. You are never permitted to rotate live API keys, alter account webhook destinations, modify payment method configurations, adjust fraud rules, or toggle capture behavior during an outage. If a credential compromise or configuration defect requires modifying our Stripe account, page Mei immediately.
3. **Disputes arrive as webhooks and are handled by Mei's team in working hours, never by on-call.**  
   A dispute webhook signifies that an end cardholder disputed a charge through their card issuer. This is normal business operations, not an operational reliability emergency. It requires review by finance and business support, never technical intervention by on-call engineers in the middle of the night.
4. **Distinguish internal latency from provider latency.**  
   The `Sorrel / payments` metrics board plots checkout latency (ours) and provider response time (theirs) side by side on the latency panel. Do not assume an elevated p95 checkout latency is an application regression until you look at the provider breakdown.
5. **No rollbacks when money has already moved.**  
   If an alert or log investigation reveals that charges, refunds, or payouts were duplicated or issued incorrectly, money has already moved. A rollback cannot pull currency back out of banking rails or card networks. The first move under the handbook is always `page owner` (Mei).

---

|               |  POST /webhooks    |  payments service   |  Mark Paid / State |                 |

|               |   Signed Payload   |  Verifies signature |                    |                 |
+---------------+                    +---------------------+                    +-----------------+
        |                                       |

        v                                       v payments DB

```

* **Stripe retries a webhook it could not deliver for up to 3 days, with growing gaps between attempts.**  
  If our ingestion endpoint returns an HTTP 5xx status, times out, or drops the connection during node maintenance or a localized database lock, Stripe queues the event and retries with an exponential backoff schedule spanning up to 72 hours.
* **Transient spikes in retries are normal.**  
  During heavy traffic windows (such as Friday evenings between 18:00 and 23:00 JST), or immediately following a regional network hiccup, Stripe may retry deliveries that took slightly longer than their timeout threshold. Seeing an uptick in retries on the `Sorrel / payments` dashboard is not an immediate catastrophe. The system is explicitly built to ingest webhooks that arrive late, out of order, or more than once.

* These payloads hit our standard webhook listener and write audit rows to the `payments` database.

## 4. Dashboards and Metrics Reference

When investigating checkout anomalies, keep the board `Sorrel / payments` open in the metrics tool alongside the corresponding region in `Sorrel / api`.

| Dashboard Panel | What It Measures | What "Normal" Looks Like | Warning Signs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Checkout Submissions & Outcomes** | Requests per minute split by region and status (success vs. failure). | Tracks customer booking curve (peaks 18:00–23:00 JST). Failures < 0.5 %. | Sharp drop in successes with failure rate > 2 % sustained over 3 minutes. |

| **Refund Volume & Amounts** | Hourly count and cumulative value of refunds issued. | Spikes slightly after 23:30 JST (daily batch refund sweep). | Sudden surge in refund count or repeated identical totals at unusual hours. |
| **Webhooks Ingestion & Retries** | Received, retried, and failed events categorized by event type. | Low steady stream of retries (< 2 %); clean acknowledgments. | Sustained 5xx responses on `/webhooks`; retry rates exceeding 10 % over an hour. |

## 5. Typical Failure Shapes and Operational Responses

In accordance with the Sorrel On-Call Handbook, you have three immediate responsibilities when an alert fires: determine the severity, choose your single first move from the five actions (`roll back`, `read logs`, `check provider`, `page owner`, `no action`), and record your initial findings in the `#inc-live` incident thread.

### 5.1 Scenario A: Upstream Outage or Degradation at Stripe

* **Observed Metrics:**  
  * The `payments-provider-timeout` rule fires.
  * More than 5 % of provider calls are timing out over a 5-minute window.
  * The latency panel shows p95 provider response time spiking sharply (e.g., > 6,000 ms), while Sorrel internal execution latency remains flat.
  * Checkout failure rate rises uniformly across all three active regions (`ap-northeast`, `us-east`, `eu-west`).
* **First Move:** `check provider`
* **Execution:**
  1. Open `status.stripe.com`. Note the exact time of their earliest reported degradation and compare it to the onset on our graphs.
  2. In the `#inc-live` incident thread, paste the alert line, state the severity, and confirm that our calls are failing due to upstream provider degradation.
  3. Subscribe the incident channel to `status.stripe.com` updates.
  4. Post an update in `#inc-live`: *"Stripe is reporting degraded performance for Charges and API. Sorrel checkout failures correlate directly with provider timeout spikes. Subscribed thread to status.stripe.com. Holding off on code changes."*
  5. If the problem persists for more than 15 minutes, the incident commander rotation will coordinate public status updates on `status.sorrel.app` using our standard templates.
  6. **Do not attempt to touch settings in the Stripe dashboard.** Wait for upstream recovery. Once Stripe stabilizes, watch the latency panel return below baseline and verify that checkout success resumes.

### 5.2 Scenario B: Elevated Webhook Retries After Recovery

* **Observed Metrics:**  
  * Following an upstream incident or a brief network blip, the `payments-webhook-retry` rule fires.
  * More than 10 % of webhooks are being retried within the hour.
  * Checkout success rate on the live site is already green and customers are booking normally.
* **First Move:** `no action` (or `read logs` if retry causes are unknown)
* **Execution:**
  1. Recall that Stripe retries a webhook it could not deliver for up to 3 days, with growing gaps between attempts.
  2. Check the `Sorrel / payments` webhook delivery panel: verify that the absolute rate of delivered events is climbing and that incoming webhooks are being successfully acknowledged (HTTP 200).
  3. Confirm that no end customers are blocked from booking appointments or completing payment flows.
  4. Classify this as a P3 event. Record the line in the on-call log noting that Stripe is draining its 3-day retry backlog following the prior disruption, and monitor the queue until it flattens.

### 5.3 Scenario C: Duplicate Charges or Abnormal Financial Movements

* **Observed Metrics:**  
  * The `payments-refund-duplicate` rule fires, or support channels flag multiple reports of customers being debited twice for a single booking reference.
  * An unexpected batch of payout transfers fires unexpectedly outside the standard Sunday 23:00 JST window.
* **First Move:** `page owner`
* **Execution:**
  1. This is an immediate P1 incident regardless of whether it affects one customer or one thousand. Money has already moved wrongly.
  2. Page Mei via the paging tool schedule. Do not rely on chat pings.
  3. Include the exact alert line, state severity P1, and summarize the symptom: *"Paging Mei: duplicate card charges confirmed for booking references. Initiating owner escalation as money has already moved."*

  5. **Never attempt to issue manual bulk refunds or change Stripe dashboard balance settings yourself.** Decisions regarding customer balance adjustments, merchant goodwill credits, and payment gateway configuration rest exclusively with Mei and finance leads.

### 5.4 Scenario D: Suspected Credential Exposure

* **Observed Metrics:**  
  * The `payments-secret-scan` rule fires indicating a pattern match for a live Stripe API secret key in application log output, an exception trace, or an admin chat export.
* **First Move:** `page owner`
* **Execution:**
  1. Live Stripe API keys are stored in our secure secrets manager and must never appear in `sorrel-prod-*` logs, tickets, or chat channels.

  4. Document the log query or reference location internally, avoiding copying the secret string into `#inc-live`.

---

## 6. Log Investigation Runbook for Payments

When debugging `payments` issues, search the index `sorrel-prod-*` in the log search tool. Ensure you constrain the search query time window to the exact minutes surrounding the alert trigger to prevent slow cluster scans.

```
# 1. Inspect top failure reasons across regions
service=payments outcome=failed region=*

# 2. Identify slow upstream calls to Stripe (> 5 seconds)
service=payments provider_ms>5000

# 3. Trace webhook ingestion lifecycle and retries
service=payments msg="webhook" outcome=retry

# 4. Check for payload validation errors on checkout
service=payments msg="validation" field=*

# 5. Trace a specific refund execution without logging card details
service=payments msg="refund sent" ref=<ref>
```

| Area / Role | Primary Contact | Secondary / Fallback | Responsibilities & Boundaries |
|---|---|---|---|
| **payments Service Owner** | Mei | Incident Commander rotation | Final authority on charges, refunds, payouts, provider configuration, dispute handling policy, and Stripe dashboard settings. |
| **API Integration & Core Engine** | Ravi | Incident Commander rotation | Manages booking states, partner integrations, database connection health, and downstream "pending payment" states. |
| **Web & Admin Portal** | Aiko | Incident Commander rotation | Manages browser checkout forms, client-side validation errors, and support admin deletion/restore flows. |
| **Platform / Infrastructure** | Kenji Sato (Platform Lead) | Sara (Platform Engineer) | Cloud networking, load balancer configuration, cross-region connectivity to Stripe endpoints. |
| **Support Lead** | Hana | Customer Support Team | Customer communication, merchant messaging, gathering report volumes during checkout disruptions. |
| **Primary On-Call Engineer** | Weekly Rotation | Assigned Secondary | First responder: triage severity, execute first move, subscribe threads to provider status, record on-call log entries. |

### Summary Checklist for payments Incidents

- [ ] Has an alert fired? Note the exact time, duration, and whether customer reports exist.
- [ ] Is Stripe itself failing? Check `status.stripe.com` and verify via the provider latency panel.
- [ ] If Stripe is degraded, subscribe the `#inc-live` incident thread to `status.stripe.com`.
- [ ] Keep hands off the Stripe dashboard. Do not toggle payment options, webhooks, or dispute configs.
- [ ] If money moved incorrectly, secrets leaked, or duplicate refunds occurred, page Mei immediately.
- [ ] Treat dispute webhooks as business-as-usual for working hours; leave them for Mei's team.
- [ ] Record the incident outcome and your first move in the on-call log after stabilization.

# twilio: Japan carrier notes

Date: 2025-03-31  
Owner: Tom (notifier)  

## Overview

Sorrel relies on twilio as our outside SMS provider for critical transactional notifications: appointment reminders, calendar updates, and one-time sign-in verification codes. The notifier service is the only Sorrel service that communicates with twilio.

Our largest operating volume originates in the `ap-northeast` region (Tokyo). Japanese telecommunications networks have unique carrier routing and reporting characteristics compared to North American or European aggregators. During high-volume morning booking periods (07:00–09:00 JST) and during evening checkout peaks, on-call engineers frequently observe metric discrepancies in delivery receipt reporting that can easily be mistaken for vendor outages.

This operational note details specific carrier behaviors in Japan—particularly regarding KDDI—to prevent false escalations and misdiagnosed alerts.

---

## Service Architecture and SMS Delivery Pipeline

Understanding the SMS lifecycle helps interpret board metrics accurately when triage is required:

1. **Queueing:** `api` or `web` enqueues an SMS payload onto notifier's background processing queue.
2. **Dispatch:** A `notifier` worker node in `ap-northeast-1` pulls the job, formats the recipient number (E.164 format, `+81`), selects the configured sender number, and issues a REST API call to twilio.
3. **Vendor Acceptance:** twilio validates the request. If accepted, twilio returns an HTTP `201 Created` with a message SID and initial status. notifier marks the message record internally as `dispatched`.
4. **Carrier Handoff:** twilio submits the SMS to the target downstream Japanese mobile carrier network (NTT Docomo, KDDI / au, SoftBank, or Rakuten Mobile).
5. **Handset Termination:** The carrier delivers the message to the customer's mobile device.
6. **Delivery Receipt (DLR):** The carrier asynchronously issues a delivery status notification back to twilio, which twilio forwards to `notifier` via an incoming status webhook. notifier processes the webhook payload and transitions the message status from `pending` to `delivered` (or `failed` / `undelivered`).

```
[ api / web ]
      │ (enqueue message)
      ▼
[ notifier worker ] ──(HTTP POST)──► [ twilio API ]
      │                                    │
      │ (dispatched)                       ▼
      │                             [ Japan Carrier ] (Docomo / KDDI / SoftBank)
      │                                    │
      │                                    ▼
      │                             [ Handset Delivered ]
      │                                    │ (Carrier DLR)
      ▼                                    ▼
[ notifier db ] ◄──(Status Webhook)─ [ twilio Webhook Router ]
(pending -> delivered)
```

## KDDI Delivery Receipt Characteristics

The primary operational anomaly observed in Japan involves the KDDI network.

### 1. Delivery Receipt Lag

- Delivery receipts for KDDI numbers in Japan can arrive up to 40 minutes after the SMS was delivered.
- While the customer often receives the SMS on their mobile device within seconds of dispatch, KDDI’s upstream aggregator and signaling network periodically batches or delays the return DLR.
- During this window, `notifier` marks such messages `pending`, not `failed`.
- Messages remain in the `pending` state until the definitive terminal status webhook is received from twilio or until internal retry/cleanup thresholds expire.

### 2. Dashboard Interpretation

On the metrics dashboard (Board **"Sorrel / notifier"**), review the channel panels carefully:

- **Pending Message Count:** A pending count rising on the notifier board for KDDI only is usually receipt lag, not failure.
- **Vendor Response Codes:** If twilio is returning standard success responses (`201`) on message creation and there is no corresponding surge in explicit vendor failure codes (`5xx` or terminal error codes), downstream delivery is taking place.
- **Oldest Message Age:** An elevated message age on delivery tracking metrics that tracks KDDI destinations alone does not indicate that worker nodes are stuck or that the queue is backing up.
- **Handset Confirmation:** Customers are generally receiving their SMS reminders without incident despite the board reflecting an accumulation of unresolved `pending` states.

```

Normal / KDDI Lag:
Twilio HTTP 201 rate:       ████████████████████ (Normal, tracking queue intake)
Twilio API 5xx rate:        (Zero)
Delivery Outcome (Docomo):  [delivered: 99%] [failed: 1%]
Delivery Outcome (KDDI):    [pending: 42%]   [delivered: 57%] [failed: 1%]
Oldest Pending Age (KDDI):  Up to 2400s (40 min)
Diagnosis:                  Carrier receipt delay. Handsets receive SMS. No action required.

True Downstream Outage:
Twilio HTTP 201 rate:       ████████████████████
Twilio API 5xx rate:        (Zero or elevated)
Delivery Outcome (KDDI):    [pending: 2%]    [undelivered/failed: 98%]
Carrier Status Page:        Incident reported on KDDI network.
Diagnosis:                  True carrier failure. Handsets not receiving SMS.
```

## Evaluating twilio Status and Carrier Status

When investigating SMS delivery anomalies or when an alert rule fires (e.g., `notifier-sms-fail`), follow standard runbook procedure: check the external dependency before altering internal configuration.

### 1. Status Page Inspection

- twilio’s status page is located at `status.twilio.com`.
- Do not rely solely on the high-level summary at the top of the page. twilio's status page lists Japanese carriers separately; check the carrier line, not only the overall status.
- Expand the **Programmable Messaging** section and look specifically under regional aggregations for Japan:
  - NTT Docomo
  - KDDI
  - SoftBank
  - Rakuten Mobile
- A major status page banner may report "Operational" globally even when a specific Japanese carrier route is degraded or suffering an unscheduled maintenance outage.

### 2. Interpreting Status Indicators

| Status Indication | Meaning for On-Call | Operational Move |
|---|---|---|
| **Global Green / KDDI Carrier Line Green** | All systems normal. If KDDI `pending` counts climb, it is standard receipt lag. | **no action** (log and monitor). |
| **Global Green / KDDI Carrier Line Degraded** | Downstream aggregator is experiencing carrier signaling queues or delayed status reports. | **check provider** (note status page timeline in `#inc-live`). Do not page owner. |
| **KDDI Carrier Line Major Outage / Failure** | Messages terminating to KDDI handsets are failing. twilio will reject or mark `undelivered`. | **check provider**. Verify impact in `#inc-live`. Support lead (Hana) handles customer messaging. |
| **Twilio API 5xx Surge (All Destinations)** | Core twilio edge platform failure. Worker dispatches failing across all carriers. | **check provider**. Verify `status.twilio.com`. Confirm retry backoff is functioning. |

---

## Administrative Ownership and Boundaries

Strict access boundaries apply to all telephony infrastructure at Sorrel. The on-call engineer, secondary on-call, and platform engineers must respect the permissions table set forth in the handbook.

- **Sender Numbers and Limits:** Sender numbers and sending limits are changed by Tom only.
- Under no circumstances should an on-call engineer attempt to provision new Japanese shortcodes, alter alphanumeric sender IDs, change twilio long-code pools, or adjust sending concurrency/throughput throttles.
- If messaging volumes approach daily or per-second account limits during high-traffic booking days, notify Tom during regular hours. Raising sending limits or purchasing additional sender numbers is a commercial and administrative decision reserved for the service owner.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ON-CALL ENGINEER                                                       │
├───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PERMITTED ACTIONS                 │ PROHIBITED ACTIONS                 │
├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Read dashboard metrics          │ • Changing sender numbers          │
│ • Inspect logs in sorrel-prod-*   │ • Purchasing new numbers           │
│ • Check status.twilio.com         │ • Modifying twilio sending limits  │
│ • Verify queue worker throughput  │ • Altering webhook URLs / secrets  │
│ • Roll back notifier deploys      │ • Contacting twilio account reps   │
│ • Document findings in #inc-live  │ • Promising customer SMS refunds   │
└───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Triage Workflow for SMS Delivery Alerts

When alerted on SMS degradation (for example, if `notifier-sms-fail` triggers because terminal failure rates exceed 20% over 5 minutes), execute the triage steps in the exact sequence specified by team doctrine.

### Step 1: Examine the Alert Context and Metrics

1. Open the board **"Sorrel / notifier"**.
2. Locate the panel **Delivery outcomes per channel (email, SMS)** and **Vendor response codes per channel**.
3. Determine whether the alert reflects actual terminal failures (`failed`, `undelivered`) or an accumulation of unconfirmed messages.
4. Check the carrier distribution:
   - If the issue affects all carriers across Japan, US, and Europe: suspect twilio API availability or our outbound networking in `ap-northeast-1`.
   - If the issue isolates strictly to KDDI recipients: check whether it is a true failure spike or elevated `pending` state accumulation.

### Step 2: Correlate Deployments

- Check deploy history in the deploy tool for service `notifier`.
- Note the age of the last deploy.
- If a new `notifier` release was deployed within the last 30 minutes, and log output indicates template rendering exceptions, payload syntax errors, or corrupted phone number formatting across all dispatches, a rollback may be warranted.
- If no recent deploy has occurred, do not touch application code or nodes.

### Step 3: Check Provider Health

- Navigate to `status.twilio.com`.
- Inspect the specific Japanese carrier status lines (NTT Docomo, KDDI, SoftBank).
- If the carrier line or messaging pipeline displays an active incident, paste the vendor update URL, incident timestamp, and details into `#inc-live`.
- Per our on-call rules, when the alert points to a third-party outage, the action is **check provider**. Rolling back application code does not restore carrier routing.

### Step 4: Examine Service Logs

Search the log indexing tool for `service=notifier`:

```
service=notifier msg="vendor error" channel=sms
```

Look for specific twilio error payloads:
- `21211`: Invalid phone number format (application or customer input issue).
- `21610`: Recipient unsubscribed/blacklisted.
- `30003` / `30005`: Handset unreachable or unknown destination.
- `30008`: Unknown carrier delivery failure (carrier-side drops).
- `Resource temporarily unavailable` or `5xx`: twilio edge gateway issues.

To monitor KDDI-specific webhook traffic:

```
service=notifier channel=sms carrier=kddi
```

Confirm whether status webhooks are arriving late with `status=delivered` or if messages are transitioning to hard delivery failures.

### Step 5: Incident Logging and Handover

Record your observation in the on-call log following standard team format:

`<date> <time JST> | notifier | <severity> | <first move> | <one sentence summary>`

*Example log entries:*
- `2025-03-31 08:15 JST | notifier | P3 | check provider | KDDI pending status count elevated on notifier board; checked status.twilio.com carrier line which confirms normal operations and standard receipt lag.`
- `2025-03-31 14:22 JST | notifier | P2 | check provider | notifier-sms-fail fired; checked status.twilio.com and identified active partial degradation on KDDI route.`

---

## Edge Cases and Failure Scenarios

### Customer Sign-In via SMS Fallback

When a true carrier outage prevents SMS delivery to Japanese handsets:
- Verification codes and one-time sign-in SMS messages will not reach the user.
- Customers attempting to log in will experience authentication blocks if they rely solely on SMS.
- The `web` authentication flow provides an email fallback mechanism. If customer inquiries escalate through support, confirm that `notifier` email dispatch via SendGrid is operational.
- Do not attempt to bypass SMS authentication at the database level. Direct all inquiries regarding authentication policies to Aiko (`web`) or Ravi (`api`).

### Nightly Batch Reminder Interaction

- Between 02:00 and 04:00 JST, notifier's scheduler generates and enqueues reminder messages for the upcoming business day across `ap-northeast`.
- Queue depth naturally rises on the **"Sorrel / notifier"** board during this period and resolves by 06:00 JST.
- If KDDI delivery receipts lag by 30 to 40 minutes during the early morning batch run, the absolute count of `pending` messages will appear unusually high due to the sheer volume dispatched in that two-hour window.
- Compare **Messages added per minute** against **Messages delivered per minute**. If workers are steadily clearing jobs from the queue and twilio returns `201 Created` for outbound dispatches, the elevated `pending` tally is benign.

---

## Escalation Reference

If an incident requires escalation beyond on-call triage:

| Scenario | Escalation Target | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent carrier failure causing wide-scale customer login failures (P1 criteria met) | Tom (notifier owner), secondary: Incident Commander rotation | Page via paging tool schedule "notifier owner" |
| Need to adjust sender numbers, messaging throughput, or twilio account limits | Tom | Ticket or direct handover during business hours |
| Inquiries regarding customer communication, status page wording, or goodwill credits | Hana (support lead) | Incident thread in `#inc-live` |
| Platform infrastructure, host networking, or outbound NAT issues in `ap-northeast-1` | Sara / Kenji Sato (platform) | Incident thread in `#inc-live` |

*Note: For any P1 incident open longer than 15 minutes, page the incident commander rotation. Do not attempt direct modification of external vendor accounts.*
